passage: Every time Vijay Chacha came over from the next village, the talk at the handpump went the same way. 'Preeti, twenty-one already. By twenty-three you should be married. passage:
Dear Salma Phuppo,

Thank you for the shawl. I'm wearing it right now in the hostel, and it still smells of your almirah.

I want to answer what you said on the phone on Sunday, because I just said "ji, ji" and then cried a bit after.

You said I should be married by twenty-three, like you were. You said I should switch from journalism to nursing because it's "safe for a girl". I know you say these things because you love me. You were the one who taught me to read the Urdu newspaper, word by word, on your verandah. That's partly why I'm studying journalism at all.

So I feel two things at once: grateful and squeezed.

I'm not switching. I'd like to finish this degree and work for a while before I think about marriage. I hope you can still be proud of me. I'll call you on Eid and tell you about my first article.

With love and respect,
Kiran

qa.q: What did Salma Phuppo say Kiran should switch to?
qa.a: She said Kiran should switch from journalism to nursing.

qa.q: What does Kiran mean by feeling "grateful and squeezed"?
qa.a: Kiran loves Phuppo and knows the advice comes from care, but the constant shoulds also feel like pressure. Both feelings are real at the same time.

qa.q: What choice does Kiran make in the letter, and why is it a respectful one?
qa.a: Kiran decides to stay with journalism and wait on marriage, but says it warmly, thanks Phuppo, and links her own choice to what Phuppo taught her. She keeps the relationship while keeping her decision.

qa.q: How might Salma Phuppo feel reading that her Urdu lessons led Kiran to journalism?
qa.a: Phuppo might feel touched and proud, and also a little torn, since the path she worries about grew from her own teaching. It could soften the pressure she puts on Kiran.

passage:
Hafsa, you asked why I went quiet when my phone buzzed. It was Aai. It's always Aai at 8 p.m.

Every call has the same three shoulds. "Nitin, you should do MBA, not this design course. You should be settled by twenty-six. You should come home more." And the funny part is, I don't even disagree with the last one.

I love her so much it's annoying. She worked double shifts at the textile mill so I could come to Pune. So when she says "should", it doesn't feel like an order. It feels like a debt.

For a year I just said "ho, Aai" and changed nothing. Then I felt guilty and angry at the same time.

Last week I tried something new. I said, "Aai, I hear you. I'm going to finish design. I'll come home every second Sunday." She was quiet. Then she said, "Every second Sunday. Promise."

She didn't agree about design. But she heard me.

qa.q: How often did Nitin promise to come home?
qa.a: Every second Sunday.

qa.q: Why does Aai's "should" feel like a debt to Nitin rather than an order?
qa.a: Nitin knows Aai worked double shifts at the mill so Nitin could study in Pune, so disagreeing feels like being ungrateful. Love and pressure are tangled together.

qa.q: What was the turning point in how Nitin handled Aai's shoulds?
qa.a: Instead of saying "ho, Aai" and changing nothing, Nitin told Aai "I hear you", stated a clear choice about design, and offered something real, coming home every second Sunday. It kept respect and choice together.

qa.q: How might Aai feel after Nitin's new answer?
qa.a: Aai may still be worried about the design course, but reassured that Nitin will come home and is being honest with her. Her "Promise" suggests she took what she could hold on to.

grounding: A young adult hears constant shoulds from Aai about course and settling down, feels love and pressure together, and finds a way to keep both respect and personal choice.

passage:
Dear Reena Apa,
It's been one of those weeks. Ammi has a new line: 'You should be married by twenty-three, like your sister.' It comes with breakfast, with the news, even with the laundry. And the other one: 'You should do B.Ed. Design is not a proper career for a girl from our family.'
The thing is, I know she means it lovingly. She stays up to heat my dinner when studio runs late. She keeps my old drawings in her cupboard. That's why it's so hard. If she were only strict, I could be angry. Instead I feel grateful and squashed at the same time.
I don't want to fight her. I want to keep having chai with her in the evenings. But I also want to finish this design course, and marry when it feels right.
How did you tell her what you wanted without hurting her?
Your little sister,
Sabina

qa.a: Ammi says Sabina should do B.Ed.

qa.a: Ammi probably sees them as protecting her daughter's future, the same care as the late dinners, and may not realise how heavy they feel.

passage:
Mridul, your Sumit chacha heard "should" more often than his own name. At twenty, in Kanpur, it was every day: "You should do engineering like your brother." "You should marry by twenty-five; the Sharma girl is good." My father said it with love. He carried cement bags so I could study. That made it harder to say no.

I felt I was letting him down just by thinking. Love and pressure on the same plate, every meal.

The turning point was an evening on the roof in mango season. I told him, "Babuji, I respect you more than anyone. I want to study agriculture, not engineering. And I will marry, but not by a date." He didn't speak for two days. Then he asked, "What will you grow?"

I became an agronomist. I married at thirty-one. He danced at the wedding.

qa.q: What did young Sumit's father do so Sumit could study?
qa.a: His father carried cement bags so Sumit could study.

qa.q: Why was it hard for young Sumit to say no to his father?
qa.a: Young Sumit felt deep love and gratitude for his father's sacrifice, so refusing felt like letting him down, even as the pressure weighed on him.

qa.q: What turning point in the story let Sumit keep both respect and his choice?
qa.a: On the roof, Sumit told his father he respected him most, then clearly named his own choices about study and marriage.

qa.q: How might Sumit's father have felt during the two days of silence?
qa.a: He was probably hurt and worried, but also thinking it over, which is why he came back with "What will you grow?"

grounding: An uncle recalls a loving father's constant shoulds about career and marriage, and keeping respect while choosing his own path.

The wedding hall in Jaipur was hot and packed, the band was deafening, and Ishita had been handed four trays of sweets to serve. Every relative she served had a "should".

"You should be next, beta. Twenty-three is the right age."
"You should take the government exam, not this start-up nonsense."

Binita Masi, fanning herself, caught her arm. "Ishu, you should let me find you someone. I only want you settled."

Ishita's throat tightened. She loved Masi; Masi had sat with her through every childhood fever. But the shoulds were piling up like the trays.

She set the tray down, knelt by Masi's chair and spoke under the music. "Masi, I know you want me happy, and that means a lot. I'm happy in my job, and I'll know when I'm ready to marry. Can you trust me a little?"

Masi blinked, then patted her cheek. "Okay. But you'll tell me first."

qa.a: Ishita felt love and pressure together, her throat tightening, because Masi meant well but the shoulds kept piling up.

passage:
For most of my first year, every phone call with Keerthana akka ended the same way. "You should switch to engineering. You should think about marriage early, like me. You should stop wasting time on history." She said it kindly. She had helped me with every exam since Class 5, and I looked up to her more than anyone. That was the problem. Her "shoulds" felt like love and like a weight at the same time.
I tried arguing. We fought. I tried agreeing. I felt hollow. Finally, one Sunday, I said, "Akka, I admire you so much. Your advice matters. But I love history, and I'm staying. Can you trust me on this one?" She was silent. Then she said, "Send me your essay. The one you got an A on." I did. She called back and said, "Okay. It's good."
It wasn't a full yes. But it was enough.
— Dhruv

qa.q: What did Keerthana akka ask Dhruv to send?
qa.a: She asked for the essay that got an A.

qa.q: Why did the constant shoulds feel so heavy to Dhruv?
qa.a: Dhruv admired and loved her, so her advice felt like care and pressure at once, which made it hard to refuse without guilt.

qa.q: What approach finally worked better than arguing or agreeing?
qa.a: Telling her with warmth that her advice mattered, while clearly stating the choice to stay with history and asking her to trust it.

qa.q: How might Keerthana akka feel after reading the essay?
qa.a: She may have felt reassured and a little proud, able to give a small yes even if she still had doubts.

passage:
Counsellor's note, the week after Diwali.
Nirmala came back from the holidays looking tired. She said the whole week at home had been "shoulds": she should switch from sociology to commerce, she should be engaged by twenty-four "like Chitra didi", she should stop wasting time on theatre. Most came from her father, Madhav, who, she says, also sat up late helping her fix her scholarship form. "He loves me. That's what makes it hard," she said. "If he were mean, I could just ignore it."
We talked about holding both: respect for his care, and her own choice. She drafted one sentence she could say calmly: "Papa, I know you want me safe. I want to finish sociology, and I'll tell you my plan."
Next: I will check in after her call home on Sunday.

qa.q: Which course did the family say Nirmala should switch to?
qa.a: Commerce.

qa.q: What was Nirmala feeling about her father's "shoulds"?
qa.a: She felt loved and pressured at once; knowing he cares made the demands harder to ignore and left her tired and torn.

qa.q: What plan did the counsellor help Nirmala make?
qa.a: One calm sentence that respects Papa's care while stating her own choice to finish sociology, with a check-in after Sunday's call home.

qa.q: How might Madhav see his "shoulds"?
qa.a: He likely sees them as care, wanting her safe and settled, the same care that kept him up late helping with her scholarship form.

grounding: A young woman hears constant shoulds from a loving father and plans a way to keep both respect and her own choice.
